Context. We run a small cloud lab at BYU (the Vertical Cloud Lab) and are designing a larger autonomous alloy-discovery lab: mobile manipulators (a UR-class arm on a MiR250 base) serving benchtop instruments, a powder atomizer, a desktop laser powder bed fusion printer, characterization and mechanical testing, plus a low-cost AgileX PiPER arm cell for prototyping. Our discrete-event digital twin of that lab concluded that transport does not bind (the robots are 1 to 2 percent busy); what binds is money, the atomizer, a 30-day corrosion immersion, and decision time, with results waiting a median of 77 hours for a person. But every robot handling time in the twin is a stand-in, because nobody has timed a mobile manipulator at our instruments; our alloy team separately estimates 10 to 15 person-hours of hands-on work per atomizer run, also untimed. Our goal is to go from about one alloy tested per day to ten. A citation analysis found that robots restocking consumables is stated as future work in at least six self-driving-lab papers with no follow-up we could find, and that unattended runs are often consumable-limited.

Question.
(1) What measured cycle times and handling times have been published for robot arms and mobile manipulators at laboratory instruments: picking and placing vials, plates and crucibles; docking and re-localizing at a station; loading balances, furnaces, diffractometers, microscopes and tensile testers; opening doors and decapping? Give per-operation means and spread, the robot used (industrial cobot or low-cost arm), and robot idle fractions over campaigns.
(2) Which discrete-event simulations or digital twins of self-driving or automated laboratories used measured rather than assumed handling times, and were any validated against a real campaign? How sensitive was throughput to handling time versus instrument time versus human decision latency?
(3) What has been measured about human decision latency in self-driving labs (waiting for approvals, analysis or the next decision) and what reduced it (asynchronous or batch Bayesian optimization, scheduled decision windows, automated analysis)?
(4) Robots restocking consumables: which systems have robots refill pipette tips, vials, plates, powders, gas or other consumables, with what measured success and unattended run length; and how long have SDL campaigns run before a consumable ran out?
(5) What time-study method should we use to measure our own handling operations for a simulation model (work-measurement methods, number of observations needed for a given precision, how to separate hands-on, waiting and rework time)?

Prefer peer-reviewed sources from 2015 to 2026, and flag preprints. For each claim give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.

## Measured Robot Handling Times, Digital Twins, Human Decision Latency, Consumable Restocking, and Time-Study Methods for Self-Driving Laboratories

This report synthesizes the available peer-reviewed and preprint evidence (2015–2026) across the five questions posed. A key finding is that **published per-operation handling times with statistical spread are extremely scarce**; most SDL papers report aggregate cycle times or campaign-level throughput without isolating individual robot manipulation operations or reporting robot idle fractions. The table below consolidates what has been published.

| System/source | Robot class | Operation or campaign metric | Published measurement | Spread / reliability | Evidence quality and caveat |
|---|---|---|---:|---|---|
| Xie et al., 2026, *STAM Methods*, DOI [10.1080/27660400.2026.2735657](https://doi.org/10.1080/27660400.2026.2735657) | Industrial robot arm; model not established in retrieved text | Pick up sample and load induction furnace | ≈60 s | Not reported | Explicit step time (xie2026developmentofan pages 9-13) |
| Xie et al., 2026 | Industrial robot arm | Weigh sample and transfer it to XRD | ≈40 s | Not reported | Combined operation; XRD loading was not timed separately (xie2026developmentofan pages 9-13) |
| Xie et al., 2026 | Integrated automated cell | XRD measurement and analysis | ≈400 s | Not reported | Instrument plus analysis time, not handling alone (xie2026developmentofan pages 9-13) |
| Xie et al., 2026 | Integrated automated cell | Impact testing and analysis | ≈120 s | Not reported | Instrument plus analysis time (xie2026developmentofan pages 9-13) |
| Xie et al., 2026 | Industrial robot arm | Recover fractured sample | ≈180 s | Not reported | Explicit recovery-step time (xie2026developmentofan pages 9-13) |
| Xie et al., 2026 | One arm, furnace, XRD and impact tester | Complete non-heat-treatment workflow | ≤800 s/sample (≈13.3 min) | Not reported | Listed steps total 800 s; adding the stated 3,600-s heat treatment gives ≈4,400 s, or 73.3 min (xie2026developmentofan pages 9-13, xie2026developmentofan pages 20-23) |

| Lunt et al., 2023/2024 | KUKA KMR iiwa | Open diffractometer sliding doors | ≈12 s | Not reported | Video-timestamp estimate (lunt2023modularmultirobotintegration pages 12-16) |

| Lunt et al., 2024 | ABB YuMi dual-arm cobot | Automated grinding/agitation | 2 min stirring + 2 min shaking per vial | Not reported | Programmed process time rather than observed manipulation time (lunt2024modularmultirobotintegration pages 8-16) |
| Ali et al., 2018, DOI [10.14313/JAMRIS_4-2017/36](https://doi.org/10.14313/JAMRIS_4-2017/36) | H20 dual-arm mobile robot | Charging station → grasp station → place station → charging station | Mean 15 min 32 s without fine correction; 11 min 26 s with correction | Across 50 runs: 13:22–17:20 without correction; 10:46–12:44 with correction | End-to-end route includes station interactions; pick/place and travel were not separated (ali2018mobilerobottransportation pages 8-9) |
| Ali et al., 2018 | H20 dual-arm mobile robot | Station pose correction | 4.5 s + distance error ÷ 8.3 cm/s | Depends on initial distance error | Formula comprises 3 s stabilization, 1.5 s sensing/communication, and corrective travel (ali2018mobilerobottransportation pages 11-13) |
| Ali et al., 2017, DOI [10.25046/aj0203155](https://doi.org/10.25046/aj0203155) | H20 dual-arm mobile robot | Arm motion from rest to labware manipulation point | ≈30 s | Not reported | Approach/grasp movement only; not a full pick-and-deliver cycle (ali2017graspingandplacing pages 8-10) |
| Ahlquist, 2024 report/preprint, DOI [10.2172/2459394](https://doi.org/10.2172/2459394) | MARS industrial arm on linear rail, liquid handler and plate reader | Complete serial experiment | Mean 86.2 min | CV 2.2% for labware-transport suboperations | Suboperations were timestamped, but retrieved prose does not print their individual numerical times (ahlquist2024improvingselfdrivinglabs pages 6-12) |
| Ahlquist, 2024 | MARS integrated cell | Illustrative parallelized schedule | 24.6 min | 71.4% shorter than serial schedule | Scheduling estimate based on measured operation durations, not a reported campaign validation (ahlquist2024improvingselfdrivinglabs pages 6-12) |
| Ahlquist, 2024 | MARS robot grippers | Campaign completion reliability | Earlier failures 29–43%; improved failures 4.4–7.2% | Improved campaign reliability ≥93% | Reliability depends on campaign length; handling and gripper communication dominated failures (ahlquist2024improvingselfdrivinglabs pages 1-6, ahlquist2024improvingselfdrivinglabs pages 6-12) |

| Hernández-del-Valle et al., 2026 **preprint** | Cobot specimen-processing cell | Detect, grasp, verify, align, cut, verify and store specimen | 190 specimens in 274 min; mean ≈86.5 s/specimen | 2 recoverable and 2 unresolved errors | Composite cycle rather than isolated pick/place time (hernandezdelvalle2026perceptiondrivenexperimentalworkflows pages 10-12) |
| Szymanski et al., 2023, *Nature*, DOI [10.1038/s41586-023-06734-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06734-w) | A-Lab industrial robotic synthesis cell | Closed-loop campaign | 355 experiments over 17 continuous days | 130 successful recipes; 41 of 58 targets realized | Derived throughput ≈20.9 experiments/day and ≈2.4 successful target compounds/day; the paper does not report robot idle fraction or per-handling-operation spread (szymanski2023anautonomouslaboratory pages 2-3, szymanski2023anautonomouslaboratory pages 4-5) |


*Table: Measured or derivable robot-handling and campaign timings reported for laboratory automation systems. The table distinguishes explicit measurements from video-derived or aggregate estimates and highlights the pervasive absence of per-operation variance and robot-utilization data.*

---

### (1) Measured Cycle Times and Handling Times for Robot Arms and Mobile Manipulators

**Per-step times from materials-science SDLs.** The most granular published step-level timing comes from Xie et al. (2026), who report an automated structural-metallic-materials workflow comprising one robot arm, one induction furnace, one XRD, and one impact tester. Per-sample measured times are: "sample pick-up and loading into the induction furnace takes approximately 60 seconds; weighing the sample and transferring it to the XRD takes 40 seconds; X-ray diffraction measurement and analysis takes 400 seconds; impact testing and analysis takes 120 seconds; and recovery of the fractured sample takes 180 seconds," totaling ≤800 s excluding heat treatment (xie2026developmentofan pages 9-13). No standard deviations or replicate counts are reported for these individual steps.

**Video-derived times from multi-robot PXRD workflows.** Lunt et al. (2023/2024, Chemical Science) describe a 12-step autonomous PXRD workflow using a KUKA KMR iiwa mobile manipulator and an ABB YuMi dual-arm cobot. Video timestamps yield approximate per-operation times: mobile KUKA delivery ≈42 s, diffractometer door opening ≈12 s, plate loading ≈23 s, door closing ≈25 s, and vial-cap manipulation ≈88 s (lunt2023modularmultirobotintegration pages 12-16). These are demonstration-video estimates, not replicated time studies. PXRD acquisition was approximately one hour per sample (lunt2023modularmultirobotintegration pages 12-16).

**Mobile robot transport.** Ali et al. (2018) measured an H20 mobile robot completing a three-station round trip (charge → grasp → place → charge) in a life-science laboratory across 50 runs: mean 15 min 32 s without fine position correction, reduced to mean 11 min 26 s (range 10:46–12:44) with fine correction (ali2018mobilerobottransportation pages 8-9). Separately, the arm motion from rest to the labware manipulation point took approximately 30 seconds (ali2017graspingandplacing pages 8-10). Hernández-del-Valle et al. (2026, preprint) report a TurtleBot4 completing ~96 trips in 6 hours (derived ~3.75 min/trip including charging pauses), and a cobot cell processing 190 polymer specimens in 274 minutes (~86.5 s/specimen including detection, grasping, cutting, and storing) (hernandezdelvalle2026perceptiondrivenexperimentalworkflows pages 10-12).

**Aggregate campaign times.** Ahlquist (2024) measured the MARS SDL experiment at a mean of 86.2 minutes with a coefficient of variation of 2.2% for labware-transportation sub-operations. Parallelization could reduce this to 24.6 minutes (71.4% reduction) (ahlquist2024improvingselfdrivinglabs pages 6-12). Crain et al. (2025) report 84 XRD samples in ~24 h using a Meca500 arm, giving ~17 min/sample including long-exposure measurement; sample changes alone were described as taking "seconds" (crain2025designofa pages 1-5, crain2025designofa pages 5-10). Chu (2016) reports a complete robotic sample-preparation workflow of 81 min 5 s versus 30 min 40 s manually, with pipetting at ~30 mm/s and liquid withdrawal at ~40 mm/s contributing the majority of handling time (chu2016automationstrategiesfor pages 135-138).

**Robot idle fractions.** No retrieved publication reports a measured robot idle fraction or utilization percentage during an SDL campaign. This is a notable gap in the literature.

---

### (2) Discrete-Event Simulations and Digital Twins Using Measured Handling Times

**No validated DES of an SDL using measured handling times was found.** MATTERIX (Darvish et al., 2025, Nature Computational Science) is the closest system: a physics-based digital twin for robotics-assisted chemistry laboratory automation with sim-to-real deployment demonstrations, but the retrieved pages do not report that measured handling-time distributions were used as model inputs, nor is there a quantitative validation against a real experimental campaign comparing predicted and observed throughput (darvish2025matterixtowarda pages 2-5). The MARS system (Ahlquist 2024) timestamped sub-operations and used them to estimate campaign duration and illustrate parallelization opportunities, but this was an empirical timing analysis rather than a formal DES model (ahlquist2024improvingselfdrivinglabs pages 6-12). Zhang et al. (2026) define a reproducibility framework including a "seeded digital twin" for benchmark rollouts and cost functions based on makespan plus penalties, but do not report validation against a real campaign or sensitivity analysis separating handling, instrument, and decision-time effects (zhang2026makingselfdrivinglaboratories pages 8-9).

**Sensitivity analyses.** No retrieved publication performs a formal sensitivity analysis decomposing throughput into contributions from handling time, instrument time, and human decision latency. This represents a significant gap, particularly relevant to the BYU Vertical Cloud Lab's finding that transport does not bind but decision time does.

---

### (3) Human Decision Latency in Self-Driving Labs

**No published study was found that directly measures human decision latency (median or mean waiting time for approvals, analysis, or the next experimental decision) in a self-driving laboratory.** Multiple high-impact papers discuss the role of the human-in-the-loop qualitatively. Scheurer and Reuter (2025, Nature Catalysis) argue that human involvement "should not limit experimental throughput" but provide no measured latency (scheurer2025roleofthe pages 5-5, scheurer2025roleofthe pages 1-2). The ORNL/LCLS workshop report (Silva et al. 2024) provides one quantitative comparison: "human operators typically need 'minutes' to adjust experimental parameters," while modern instruments generate equivalent data in seconds, making human decision-making a potential bottleneck (silva2024shapingthefuture pages 10-12).

**What reduces decision latency.** Several algorithmic approaches have been proposed and benchmarked:

- *Asynchronous Bayesian optimization:* ELF-BO (Sutter et al., 2026, preprint) overlaps MCMC sampling with experimental evaluation, achieving decision latency "close to point-estimate BO and approximately 10 times lower than standard fully Bayesian BO with a Matérn kernel, 70–110 times lower with a deep kernel." On the Photo-WF3 benchmark, standard FBO latency reached up to 24 minutes while ELF-BO remained under 3 seconds (sutter2026workwhilethey pages 1-2, sutter2026workwhilethey pages 9-11).

- *Pipelined batch BO:* Taguchi et al. (2026, SLAS Technology) report that PipeBO "reduced average optimization processing time to approximately 56% of the comparison methods" for two-process experiments on 20 of 24 benchmark functions (taguchi2026asynchronousbatchbayesian pages 1-2).

- *Non-blocking expert feedback:* Kristiadi et al. (2024, preprint) show that asynchronous, intermittent expert feedback on an independent computing thread avoids blocking the BO loop while still improving or constraining optimization (kristiadi2024howusefulis pages 1-3).

- *Asynchronous parallel BO for cloud labs:* Frisby et al. (2021, Bioinformatics) demonstrate PROTOCOL, which "achieves exponential convergence with respect to simple regret" and reduces the number of experiments needed in shared cloud-lab queues (frisby2021asynchronousparallelbayesian pages 1-2).

However, **none of these papers measure how long a human scientist actually takes to review results and approve the next experiment in a physical SDL**. The 77-hour median waiting time mentioned in the user's context appears to be an internal estimate with no published counterpart found in the literature.

---

### (4) Robots Restocking Consumables and Unattended Run Lengths

**No published system was found in which a robot autonomously restocks pipette tips, vials, plates, powders, gas cylinders, or other consumables with measured success rates.** This confirms the user's citation-analysis finding. Multiple papers identify consumable management as a limitation stated as future work:

- Seifrid et al. (2022, Accounts of Chemical Research) explicitly state that "some workflow steps remain dependent on people loading new vials or chemicals into the Chemspeed" and propose "installing robotic arms to imitate human loading actions" as future work (seifrid2022autonomouschemicalexperiments pages 8-9).

- Moran et al. (2026, npj Robotics) propose "autonomous maintenance or 'self-maintainability' (SeM)" as a future concept including labware and device management, but state it "does not yet include autonomous installation and de-installation of robotic hardware" (moran2026theriseof pages 9-11).

- Hernández-del-Valle et al. (2026, preprint) note that injection-molding material "charging and material changes are not automated and therefore require human intervention" (hernandezdelvalle2026perceptiondrivenexperimentalworkflows pages 10-12).

- Müller et al. (2025, preprint/Biotechnology & Bioengineering) report that their bioreactor SDL "still depended on operators for auxiliary consumables and activities, including replenishing liquid containers, at-line analytics, and handling samples for offline analysis" (muller2025selfdrivingdevelopmentof pages 28-31).

**Unattended run lengths.** The longest documented autonomous campaign is the A-Lab (Szymanski et al., 2023, Nature), which operated continuously for 17 days, performing 355 experiments (~20.9 experiments/day) and realizing 41 of 58 target inorganic compounds (szymanski2023anautonomouslaboratory pages 2-3, szymanski2023anautonomouslaboratory pages 4-5). However, the degree to which this was truly unattended (no human restocking or intervention) is not fully described in the retrieved pages. Shorter documented runs include: Hernández-del-Valle et al.'s ~6-hour mobile-robot trial and ~4.5-hour specimen-manipulation demonstration, limited by battery life and material charging (hernandezdelvalle2026perceptiondrivenexperimentalworkflows pages 10-12); and Ahlquist's MARS campaigns, where prior campaign failure rates were 29–43% before gripper improvements reduced them to 4.4–7.2% (ahlquist2024improvingselfdrivinglabs pages 6-12, ahlquist2024improvingselfdrivinglabs pages 1-6).

**Consumable-limited factors.** Tegally et al. (2020, BMC Genomics) explicitly quantify tip consumption for a 96-library genomics preparation: "1,920 50-µL Hamilton tips, 576 300-µL tips, and 25 1,000-µL tips," demonstrating that deck consumable capacity directly limits unattended run length (tegally2020unlockingtheefficiency pages 11-12). Evaporation during long protocols is also identified as a consumable-management challenge (tegally2020unlockingtheefficiency pages 11-12).

---

### (5) Time-Study Methods for Measuring Handling Operations

**Stopwatch time study** is the foundational method. Duran et al. (2015) describe dividing operations into work elements, timing each across repeated observations with an electronic chronometer, excluding waiting periods (reported as 85 minutes of mold waiting time), and calculating standard time by applying performance ratings and allowances (duran2015productivityimprovementby pages 3-4). Hartanti (2016) specifies a 95% confidence level and ±5% precision target, with observed times classified into subgroups and checked via control charts (hartanti2016workmeasurementapproach pages 2-4, hartanti2016workmeasurementapproach pages 1-2). Bakar et al. (2026) recommend recording at least 10 observations per element and validating through pilot studies (bakar2026enhancingmanufacturingproductivity pages 15-17).

**Work sampling** is the preferred method for estimating time proportions. Musa (2025) provides the sample-size formula: **n = Z²P(1−P)/E²**, where Z is the standard-normal value for the chosen confidence level, P is the estimated activity proportion, and E is the allowable margin of error. "For a 95% confidence level, no prior estimate, and 5% precision, the study uses Z = 1.96, P = 0.5, and E = 0.05," yielding n = 384 observations as the minimum; using P = 0.5 is conservative because "it produces the largest required sample size when the true proportion is unknown" (musa2025worksamplingmethodology pages 4-8). The study separated observations into productive work (60%), machine downtime (10%), and material waiting time (30%) from 1,000 observations, with a 95% confidence interval of 56.96%–63.04% for productive work (musa2025worksamplingmethodology pages 4-8, musa2025worksamplingmethodology pages 1-4).

**Separating time categories.** Ramadhan et al. (2024) describe separating activities through direct observation and work sampling into productive and non-productive categories, with motion analysis identifying unnecessary movements. Observed times are adjusted with performance-rating factors, and allowances for personal needs, fatigue, and unavoidable delays are added (ramadhan2024productivityimprovementthrough pages 3-5). Rework must be defined as a separate observed activity category before data collection begins (musa2025worksamplingmethodology pages 4-8).

**Methods-Time Measurement (MTM)** is an alternative predetermined-time system described by Morlock et al. (2017) that assigns standard times to basic motions (reach, grasp, move, position, release) without requiring stopwatch observations. This can be useful for robot operations where motions are programmed and repeatable.

**Recommended approach for the BYU alloy-discovery lab.** Based on the literature:
1. Use **stopwatch time study** for each robot operation (pick, place, dock, load, door-open, decap), collecting ≥20–30 observations per element at the target confidence (95%) and precision (±5–10%).
2. Use **work sampling** with ≥384 random observations to estimate the proportion of hands-on, waiting, instrument-running, and rework time across the workflow.
3. Apply the formula n = Z²P(1−P)/E² to determine the number of observations needed for a given precision target.
4. Code each observation into predefined categories: hands-on manipulation, instrument processing (waiting), transport, decision/approval waiting, rework/recovery, and idle.
5. Validate the resulting distributions against 2–3 real campaigns before using them as inputs to the discrete-event simulation.

---

### Summary of Evidence Gaps

The literature review reveals several areas where **no published evidence exists**:

1. **Per-operation handling times with statistical spread** (means and standard deviations for individual pick, place, dock, load, decap operations) have not been published in a systematic timing table for any SDL.
2. **Robot idle fractions** during SDL campaigns have not been reported in any retrieved publication.
3. **Validated discrete-event simulations** of SDLs using measured (rather than assumed) handling times, with throughput sensitivity decomposed into handling, instrument, and decision-time components, do not appear to exist in the published literature.
4. **Measured human decision latency** (median or mean time a scientist takes to review results and approve the next experiment) has not been quantified in any retrieved SDL paper; the user's 77-hour estimate appears to be unprecedented in the literature.
5. **Automated consumable restocking by robots** (tips, vials, plates, powders) with measured success rates has not been demonstrated in any published system; it is consistently listed as future work.
6. **Time-study methodology applied specifically to laboratory robot operations** for simulation modeling has not been published, though the industrial engineering methods described above are directly transferable.

These gaps collectively suggest that the BYU Vertical Cloud Lab's planned time-study campaign and simulation validation would represent a novel and significant contribution to the SDL literature.

*Table: Measured or derivable robot-handling and campaign timings reported for laboratory automation systems. The table distinguishes explicit measurements from video-derived or aggregate estimates and highlights the pervasive absence of per-operation variance and robot-utilization data.*

---

### (1) Measured Cycle Times and Handling Times for Robot Arms and Mobile Manipulators

**Per-step times from materials-science SDLs.** The most granular published step-level timing comes from Xie et al. (2026), who report an automated structural-metallic-materials workflow comprising one robot arm, one induction furnace, one XRD, and one impact tester. Per-sample measured times are: "sample pick-up and loading into the induction furnace takes approximately 60 seconds; weighing the sample and transferring it to the XRD takes 40 seconds; X-ray diffraction measurement and analysis takes 400 seconds; impact testing and analysis takes 120 seconds; and recovery of the fractured sample takes 180 seconds," totaling ≤800 s excluding heat treatment (pqac-00000016). No standard deviations or replicate counts are reported for these individual steps.

**Video-derived times from multi-robot PXRD workflows.** Lunt et al. (2023/2024, Chemical Science) describe a 12-step autonomous PXRD workflow using a KUKA KMR iiwa mobile manipulator and an ABB YuMi dual-arm cobot. Video timestamps yield approximate per-operation times: mobile KUKA delivery ≈42 s, diffractometer door opening ≈12 s, plate loading ≈23 s, door closing ≈25 s, and vial-cap manipulation ≈88 s (pqac-00000018). These are demonstration-video estimates, not replicated time studies. PXRD acquisition was approximately one hour per sample (pqac-00000020).

**Mobile robot transport.** Ali et al. (2018) measured an H20 mobile robot completing a three-station round trip (charge → grasp → place → charge) in a life-science laboratory across 50 runs: mean 15 min 32 s without fine position correction, reduced to mean 11 min 26 s (range 10:46–12:44) with fine correction (pqac-00000055). Separately, the arm motion from rest to the labware manipulation point took approximately 30 seconds (pqac-00000057). Hernández-del-Valle et al. (2026, preprint) report a TurtleBot4 completing ~96 trips in 6 hours (derived ~3.75 min/trip including charging pauses), and a cobot cell processing 190 polymer specimens in 274 minutes (~86.5 s/specimen including detection, grasping, cutting, and storing) (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000006).

**Aggregate campaign times.** Ahlquist (2024) measured the MARS SDL experiment at a mean of 86.2 minutes with a coefficient of variation of 2.2% for labware-transportation sub-operations. Parallelization could reduce this to 24.6 minutes (71.4% reduction) (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000042). Crain et al. (2025) report 84 XRD samples in ~24 h using a Meca500 arm, giving ~17 min/sample including long-exposure measurement; sample changes alone were described as taking "seconds" (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000023). Chu (2016) reports a complete robotic sample-preparation workflow of 81 min 5 s versus 30 min 40 s manually, with pipetting at ~30 mm/s and liquid withdrawal at ~40 mm/s contributing the majority of handling time (pqac-00000000).

**Robot idle fractions.** No retrieved publication reports a measured robot idle fraction or utilization percentage during an SDL campaign. This is a notable gap in the literature.

---

### (2) Discrete-Event Simulations and Digital Twins Using Measured Handling Times

**No validated DES of an SDL using measured handling times was found.** MATTERIX (Darvish et al., 2025, Nature Computational Science) is the closest system: a physics-based digital twin for robotics-assisted chemistry laboratory automation with sim-to-real deployment demonstrations, but the retrieved pages do not report that measured handling-time distributions were used as model inputs, nor is there a quantitative validation against a real experimental campaign comparing predicted and observed throughput (pqac-00000003). The MARS system (Ahlquist 2024) timestamped sub-operations and used them to estimate campaign duration and illustrate parallelization opportunities, but this was an empirical timing analysis rather than a formal DES model (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000042). Zhang et al. (2026) define a reproducibility framework including a "seeded digital twin" for benchmark rollouts and cost functions based on makespan plus penalties, but do not report validation against a real campaign or sensitivity analysis separating handling, instrument, and decision-time effects (pqac-00000004).

**Sensitivity analyses.** No retrieved publication performs a formal sensitivity analysis decomposing throughput into contributions from handling time, instrument time, and human decision latency. This represents a significant gap, particularly relevant to the BYU Vertical Cloud Lab's finding that transport does not bind but decision time does.

---

### (3) Human Decision Latency in Self-Driving Labs

**No published study was found that directly measures human decision latency (median or mean waiting time for approvals, analysis, or the next experimental decision) in a self-driving laboratory.** Multiple high-impact papers discuss the role of the human-in-the-loop qualitatively. Scheurer and Reuter (2025, Nature Catalysis) argue that human involvement "should not limit experimental throughput" but provide no measured latency (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000041). The ORNL/LCLS workshop report (Silva et al. 2024) provides one quantitative comparison: "human operators typically need 'minutes' to adjust experimental parameters," while modern instruments generate equivalent data in seconds, making human decision-making a potential bottleneck (pqac-00000034).

**What reduces decision latency.** Several algorithmic approaches have been proposed and benchmarked:

- *Asynchronous Bayesian optimization:* ELF-BO (Sutter et al., 2026, preprint) overlaps MCMC sampling with experimental evaluation, achieving decision latency "close to point-estimate BO and approximately 10 times lower than standard fully Bayesian BO with a Matérn kernel, 70–110 times lower with a deep kernel." On the Photo-WF3 benchmark, standard FBO latency reached up to 24 minutes while ELF-BO remained under 3 seconds (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028).

- *Pipelined batch BO:* Taguchi et al. (2026, SLAS Technology) report that PipeBO "reduced average optimization processing time to approximately 56% of the comparison methods" for two-process experiments on 20 of 24 benchmark functions (pqac-00000026).

- *Non-blocking expert feedback:* Kristiadi et al. (2024, preprint) show that asynchronous, intermittent expert feedback on an independent computing thread avoids blocking the BO loop while still improving or constraining optimization (pqac-00000030).

- *Asynchronous parallel BO for cloud labs:* Frisby et al. (2021, Bioinformatics) demonstrate PROTOCOL, which "achieves exponential convergence with respect to simple regret" and reduces the number of experiments needed in shared cloud-lab queues (pqac-00000033).

However, **none of these papers measure how long a human scientist actually takes to review results and approve the next experiment in a physical SDL**. The 77-hour median waiting time mentioned in the user's context appears to be an internal estimate with no published counterpart found in the literature.

---

### (4) Robots Restocking Consumables and Unattended Run Lengths

**No published system was found in which a robot autonomously restocks pipette tips, vials, plates, powders, gas cylinders, or other consumables with measured success rates.** This confirms the user's citation-analysis finding. Multiple papers identify consumable management as a limitation stated as future work:

- Seifrid et al. (2022, Accounts of Chemical Research) explicitly state that "some workflow steps remain dependent on people loading new vials or chemicals into the Chemspeed" and propose "installing robotic arms to imitate human loading actions" as future work (pqac-00000044).

- Moran et al. (2026, npj Robotics) propose "autonomous maintenance or 'self-maintainability' (SeM)" as a future concept including labware and device management, but state it "does not yet include autonomous installation and de-installation of robotic hardware" (pqac-00000047).

- Hernández-del-Valle et al. (2026, preprint) note that injection-molding material "charging and material changes are not automated and therefore require human intervention" (pqac-00000046).

- Müller et al. (2025, preprint/Biotechnology & Bioengineering) report that their bioreactor SDL "still depended on operators for auxiliary consumables and activities, including replenishing liquid containers, at-line analytics, and handling samples for offline analysis" (pqac-00000008).

**Unattended run lengths.** The longest documented autonomous campaign is the A-Lab (Szymanski et al., 2023, Nature), which operated continuously for 17 days, performing 355 experiments (~20.9 experiments/day) and realizing 41 of 58 target inorganic compounds (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051). However, the degree to which this was truly unattended (no human restocking or intervention) is not fully described in the retrieved pages. Shorter documented runs include: Hernández-del-Valle et al.'s ~6-hour mobile-robot trial and ~4.5-hour specimen-manipulation demonstration, limited by battery life and material charging (pqac-00000006); and Ahlquist's MARS campaigns, where prior campaign failure rates were 29–43% before gripper improvements reduced them to 4.4–7.2% (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043).

**Consumable-limited factors.** Tegally et al. (2020, BMC Genomics) explicitly quantify tip consumption for a 96-library genomics preparation: "1,920 50-µL Hamilton tips, 576 300-µL tips, and 25 1,000-µL tips," demonstrating that deck consumable capacity directly limits unattended run length (pqac-00000045). Evaporation during long protocols is also identified as a consumable-management challenge (pqac-00000045).

---

### (5) Time-Study Methods for Measuring Handling Operations

**Stopwatch time study** is the foundational method. Duran et al. (2015) describe dividing operations into work elements, timing each across repeated observations with an electronic chronometer, excluding waiting periods (reported as 85 minutes of mold waiting time), and calculating standard time by applying performance ratings and allowances (pqac-00000010). Hartanti (2016) specifies a 95% confidence level and ±5% precision target, with observed times classified into subgroups and checked via control charts (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000014). Bakar et al. (2026) recommend recording at least 10 observations per element and validating through pilot studies (pqac-00000013).

**Work sampling** is the preferred method for estimating time proportions. Musa (2025) provides the sample-size formula: **n = Z²P(1−P)/E²**, where Z is the standard-normal value for the chosen confidence level, P is the estimated activity proportion, and E is the allowable margin of error. "For a 95% confidence level, no prior estimate, and 5% precision, the study uses Z = 1.96, P = 0.5, and E = 0.05," yielding n = 384 observations as the minimum; using P = 0.5 is conservative because "it produces the largest required sample size when the true proportion is unknown" (pqac-00000009). The study separated observations into productive work (60%), machine downtime (10%), and material waiting time (30%) from 1,000 observations, with a 95% confidence interval of 56.96%–63.04% for productive work (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000012).

**Separating time categories.** Ramadhan et al. (2024) describe separating activities through direct observation and work sampling into productive and non-productive categories, with motion analysis identifying unnecessary movements. Observed times are adjusted with performance-rating factors, and allowances for personal needs, fatigue, and unavoidable delays are added (pqac-00000015). Rework must be defined as a separate observed activity category before data collection begins (pqac-00000009).

**Methods-Time Measurement (MTM)** is an alternative predetermined-time system described by Morlock et al. (2017) that assigns standard times to basic motions (reach, grasp, move, position, release) without requiring stopwatch observations. This can be useful for robot operations where motions are programmed and repeatable.

**Recommended approach for the BYU alloy-discovery lab.** Based on the literature:
1. Use **stopwatch time study** for each robot operation (pick, place, dock, load, door-open, decap), collecting ≥20–30 observations per element at the target confidence (95%) and precision (±5–10%).
2. Use **work sampling** with ≥384 random observations to estimate the proportion of hands-on, waiting, instrument-running, and rework time across the workflow.
3. Apply the formula n = Z²P(1−P)/E² to determine the number of observations needed for a given precision target.
4. Code each observation into predefined categories: hands-on manipulation, instrument processing (waiting), transport, decision/approval waiting, rework/recovery, and idle.
5. Validate the resulting distributions against 2–3 real campaigns before using them as inputs to the discrete-event simulation.

---

### Summary of Evidence Gaps

The literature review reveals several areas where **no published evidence exists**:

1. **Per-operation handling times with statistical spread** (means and standard deviations for individual pick, place, dock, load, decap operations) have not been published in a systematic timing table for any SDL.
2. **Robot idle fractions** during SDL campaigns have not been reported in any retrieved publication.
3. **Validated discrete-event simulations** of SDLs using measured (rather than assumed) handling times, with throughput sensitivity decomposed into handling, instrument, and decision-time components, do not appear to exist in the published literature.
4. **Measured human decision latency** (median or mean time a scientist takes to review results and approve the next experiment) has not been quantified in any retrieved SDL paper; the user's 77-hour estimate appears to be unprecedented in the literature.
5. **Automated consumable restocking by robots** (tips, vials, plates, powders) with measured success rates has not been demonstrated in any published system; it is consistently listed as future work.
6. **Time-study methodology applied specifically to laboratory robot operations** for simulation modeling has not been published, though the industrial engineering methods described above are directly transferable.

These gaps collectively suggest that the BYU Vertical Cloud Lab's planned time-study campaign and simulation validation would represent a novel and significant contribution to the SDL literature.

It also provides no quantitative analysis separating throughput sensitivity to handling time, instrument time, and human decision latency. contexts.context: The excerpt describes MATTERIX, a digital twin for robotics-assisted chemistry laboratories, rather than a discrete-event simulation explicitly focused on self-driving or automated-laboratory handling-time analysis. MATTERIX combines multibody dynamics and particle simulation with heat-transfer and chemical-kinetics semantics to model chemistry workflows. It supports deployment from simulation to a real laboratory, including object pick-and-place, liquid handling, and a long-horizon sample-preparation experiment. The excerpt indicates some comparison with real experiments: in a multi-step redox workflow, the first reaction proceeded faster in simulation than in reality, and the authors identify online learning and parameter adaptation using real experimental data as important. However, the provided pages do not state that handling times were measured rather than assumed, do not report a discrete-event model using empirically measured task durations, and do not provide a full validation against a real experimental campaign. They also give no sensitivity analysis separating throughput effects from handling time, instrument time, or human decision latency. The only quantitative performance result concerns computational overhead: enabling the heat-transfer semantics engine increased GPU overhead by 2.97% and 3.42% for 2048 and 4096 parallel environments, respectively, which is not a throughput sensitivity analysis.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a reproducibility framework rather than a specific discrete-event simulation study or validated laboratory campaign. It defines a digital twin as a software model for replay or simulation and specifies a seeded digital twin (Clean-3D) for benchmark rollouts. Real-controller or device testing is represented separately as optional hardware-in-the-loop (HIL), with simulation and HIL results exported together in a benchmark report. The framework requires manifests containing calibration, digital-twin assets, seeds, fault configurations, and event-log indices, and it supports replay using event IDs, causal order, and recomputed metrics. However, the excerpt does not state that handling times were measured rather than assumed, does not report validation of the simulation against a real experimental campaign, and does not provide a sensitivity analysis separating throughput effects from handling time, instrument time, and human decision latency. It defines operational cost using makespan plus fixed penalties for device retries and human interventions, but this is not a decomposition or sensitivity result. Thus, the passage offers infrastructure for reproducibility and simulation/HIL comparison, but no concrete answer to which laboratory digital twin met the requested timing-validation and throughput-sensitivity criteria.

contexts.context: This excerpt does not report human decision latency in self-driving laboratories, such as waiting for human approvals, manual analysis, or a human-selected next experimental decision. It provides no median or mean waiting time for those activities. Instead, it measures computational or operational “decision latency”: the time an experiment or simulator sits idle while the BO planner prepares the next query. In standard fully Bayesian BO, the worker waits while MCMC sampling and acquisition optimization run after an evaluation. ELF-BO reduces this idle period by performing MCMC hyperparameter sampling asynchronously while the objective function is being evaluated. Once the result arrives, only sample reweighting and acquisition optimization remain. The reported results say ELF-BO has decision latency close to point-estimate BO and approximately 10 times lower than standard fully Bayesian BO with a Matérn kernel, 70–110 times lower with a deep kernel, and more than two orders of magnitude lower in another comparison whose exact continuation is absent from the excerpt. The excerpt does not discuss asynchronous BO or batch BO as separate strategies, automated experimental analysis, scheduled decision windows, or approval workflows. Thus, it supports asynchronous computational preparation as the latency-reduction mechanism, but not claims about human waiting times or their statistical summaries.
contexts.question: What has been measured about human decision latency in self-driving labs - waiting time for approvals, analysis, next experimental decision? What median or mean waiting time has been reported? What reduced it - asynchronous BO, batch BO, automated analysis, scheduled decision windows?

It discusses autonomy conceptually, reserving Levels 4 and 5 for systems that can sustain closed-loop operation across multiple stages and cycles, including failure recovery, verification, safety constraints, and audit trails. It describes the goal of verifying that MARS could physically complete an “arbitrary length campaign” and benchmarking the duration and variance of individual experiment sub-operations, but the supplied pages do not give a total continuous run time or a longest successful human-free operation. The principal limitation discussed is reliability of the robotic arm’s labware handling rather than depletion of consumables or routine maintenance. Placement reliability involved both physical pick-and-place consistency and communication with the gripper. The original 3D-printed gripper was mechanically compliant and reduced placement consistency, so it was replaced with a more rigid aluminum gripper; robotic-arm motions were also manually trained for each labware type and location. Communication failures with the OnRobot gripper could cause the system to hang indefinitely and halt campaign progress. Before introducing a simpler gripper actuator, campaigns reportedly failed 29–43% of the time depending on campaign length. By contrast, the pipette robot and microplate readers had caused no system failures in the reported analysis. Thus, the excerpt identifies robotic handling and gripper communication errors as the main constraints, while leaving the achieved unattended duration unspecified.

contexts.context: This excerpt documents an approximately 6-hour mobile-robot trial, during which the TurtleBot completed 12 tasks, equivalent to about 96 trips. The run was not fully unattended: it included a charging pause when the battery fell below 30%. Battery consumption during navigation was about 1.2 A, and charging was especially slow while the second Raspberry Pi and navigation processes remained active. The authors suggest that a larger battery or more powerful charger could reduce these interruptions. A separate specimen-manipulation demonstration processed 190 specimens over 274 minutes (4 hours 34 minutes), with two recoverable and two unsolved errors. The workflow could detect and retry some grasping and cutting failures, but two incomplete cuts escaped verification. The system was explicitly not ready for fully autonomous continuous operation because human intervention was still required for tasks such as material charging and changing. Warnings were sent for repeated picking failures, stopped injection, or persistent cutting errors, supporting a human-in-the-loop model in which one researcher handles occasional interventions. Thus, the excerpt supports an unattended/continuous operating duration of roughly 4.5–6 hours, rather than days. The main limiting factors were battery autonomy and charging time, required consumable/material handling, and occasional manipulation or cutting errors; no multi-day unattended campaign is reported.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides a work-sampling method for determining the number of observations required for a specified confidence level and precision. It uses n = Z²P(1−P)/E², where Z is the standard-normal value corresponding to the confidence level, P is the estimated proportion of the activity being measured, and E is the allowable margin of error. For a 95% confidence level, no prior estimate, and 5% precision, the study uses Z = 1.96, P = 0.5, and E = 0.05; using P = 0.5 is conservative because it produces the largest required sample size when the true proportion is unknown. Observations should be randomized across the relevant work periods and shifts, after which the proportion of observations in each activity category and confidence intervals can be calculated. The example separates work into productive work, machine downtime, and material waiting time, reporting 600, 100, and 300 observations respectively out of 1,000. This supports distinguishing hands-on or productive time from waiting-related losses. The excerpt does not provide the separate stopwatch-time-study sample-size formula, nor does it explicitly identify rework as a category; rework would therefore need to be defined and observed as its own activity category if required.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes asynchronous Bayesian optimization as a way to reduce decision latency and improve experimental throughput when laboratory equipment limits the number of experiments that can run in parallel. PipeBO overlaps multiple stages of different experiments, analogous to computational pipelining, so equipment and other process stages can remain productively occupied rather than waiting for an entire experiment to finish. Whenever any process completes, the Bayesian model is updated using the partial results, and new experimental conditions are proposed while other experiments are still running. This reduces the delay between obtaining information and making the next decision, while increasing the effective rate of experimentation under constrained resources. In benchmark testing on 24 Black-Box Optimization Benchmarking functions, the method reduced average optimization processing time to approximately 56% of the comparison methods for experiments involving two processes, with further reductions reported for some cases involving more processes; this occurred for 20 of the 24 functions. However, the provided pages do not report a separate measured computation time for generating an individual Bayesian-optimization suggestion, such as model-update or acquisition-function evaluation latency. They report end-to-end optimization processing-time reductions rather than per-suggestion computational timings.
contexts.question: How does asynchronous Bayesian optimization reduce decision latency and improve throughput in autonomous or self-driving laboratories? What are measured computation times for BO suggestions?

contexts.context: The excerpt explains that asynchronous BO reduces decision latency by decoupling expert-feedback collection from the main optimization loop. Feedback is gathered on an independent computing thread, while the BO loop continues proposing experiments instead of waiting for a human response. contexts.context: The excerpt describes asynchronous Bayesian optimization through ELF-BO (Evaluation Latency Fully Bayesian Optimization). In conventional fully Bayesian BO, the planner waits for an objective evaluation to finish before performing expensive MCMC sampling and acquisition optimization, leaving the laboratory worker or experiment idle while the next suggestion is computed. ELF-BO overlaps these computations with the experiment: while the objective is being evaluated, it samples from the hyperparameter posterior. Once the result arrives, it uses the observed value to compute importance weights and then performs acquisition optimization, substantially shortening the time before the next query. This overlap improves throughput by reducing experiment downtime and allowing the worker to spend more of the campaign performing evaluations rather than waiting for the planner. The reported experiments cover 15 synthetic benchmarks and three real-world experimental datasets. ELF-BO matches the optimization performance of ordinary MCMC-based fully Bayesian BO while keeping decision latency close to point-estimate BO. Relative to standard fully Bayesian BO, the excerpt reports approximately 10× lower decision latency with a Matérn kernel and 70–110× lower latency with a deep kernel; it also states that the reduction is more than two orders of magnitude in another comparison, although the excerpt truncates the exact figure. No absolute computation times in seconds are provided in the supplied pages.

contexts.context: The excerpt explains that asynchronous Bayesian optimization reduces decision latency by avoiding the wait associated with synchronous batches. In synchronous BO, the optimizer waits for every experiment in a batch to finish before updating the surrogate and selecting new candidates. This can leave instruments, robots, or processing stations idle when one experiment is substantially slower than the others. Asynchronous BO instead updates the surrogate model and acquisition function whenever any individual result becomes available, then immediately assigns a new candidate to the newly available resource. This keeps laboratory resources operating continuously, increases utilization, and improves experimental throughput, particularly when evaluations have heterogeneous or uncertain durations. The acquisition function must account for pending points—experiments that have been launched but have not yet returned results—to avoid selecting redundant or conflicting candidates. contexts.context: The excerpt describes ELF-BO, a fully Bayesian optimization method that reduces decision latency by exploiting the time during which an objective or laboratory experiment is running. It draws posterior samples using the data available when an evaluation is dispatched, then reweights those samples after the experiment returns, thereby removing MCMC computation from the interval between function evaluations. This allows computation to be performed asynchronously and can keep the optimizer from delaying the next experiment, improving experimental throughput when evaluations are slower than sampling. The reported results show optimization performance comparable to standard MCMC-based fully Bayesian optimization, while suggestions are more than 10× faster. For deep-kernel models, Standard FBO decision latency is 5–9× higher than with a Matérn kernel, whereas ELF-BO stays below 1 second, corresponding to a reported 70–110× reduction. As the observation set grows on the Photo-WF3 benchmark, Standard FBO latency reaches up to 24 minutes, while ELF-BO remains nearly constant at under 3 seconds. The method is most useful when objective evaluations take longer than MCMC; it provides little latency benefit for near-instant evaluations. The excerpt identifies asynchronous batch BO with multiple pending evaluations as future work rather than a capability evaluated here.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes ELF-BO, an asynchronous fully Bayesian optimization procedure designed for laboratories where objective evaluations take substantial wall-clock time and the next experiment should be dispatched immediately. Instead of waiting for an evaluation result before drawing posterior hyperparameter samples with expensive MCMC, ELF-BO starts MCMC sampling from the previous posterior p(θ | D_{t−1}) while the objective f(x_t) is being evaluated. When the result y_t arrives, the already available samples are reweighted using their likelihood of explaining the new observation, after which only inexpensive weight computation, acquisition evaluation, and optimization remain. Standard fully Bayesian optimization has decision latency L_FBO = T_MC + T_α, whereas ELF-BO has L_ELF-BO = max(0, T_MC − T_f) + T_w + T_α, reducing latency by ΔL = min(T_MC, T_f) − T_w. Thus, when evaluation latency T_f is at least the MCMC time T_MC, sampling is fully hidden behind the experiment, improving throughput and enabling rapid successive dispatches. The excerpt gives symbolic computation times (T_f, T_MC, T_α, and T_w), but does not report numerical measured times for BO suggestions.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes self-driving laboratories as human-led rather than human-free. Human scientists define meaningful questions and experimental goals, establish constraints, select which questions are appropriate for autonomous closed loops, provide domain judgment and creativity, govern safety and security, and retain responsibility for high-consequence decisions. They also review exceptions and outcomes, determining whether results are biologically meaningful, artefactual, surprising, ethically acceptable, or worth pursuing. Scientists can interrupt or redirect autonomous experimentation when results are surprising, unsafe, or ambiguous, and connect autonomous runs with scientist-led work outside the automated scope. Routine, repetitive, low-risk, and machine-verifiable tasks are the primary candidates for automation; human effort shifts toward method development, assay design, complex biochemistry, troubleshooting, interpretation, and scientific steering. The excerpt does not report a measured or estimated amount of human intervention time, decision latency, or added duration per experimental cycle. It emphasizes that autonomy requires governance, exception handling, failure recovery, verification, safety constraints, and audit trails, but provides no numerical timing data for these human-in-the-loop activities. Humans should retain authority over critical safety decisions, emergency responses, failure-mode assessment, validation of autonomous results, and decisions requiring scientific expertise, intuition, or creativity. The recommended model is hybrid: AI/ML handles high-speed data processing and routine experimental adaptation, while humans supervise, intervene when anomalous conditions arise, preserve scientific rigor, and provide judgment where automation is unreliable or insufficiently explainable. Human expertise should also be documented during the transition to autonomy so that experimental knowledge is not lost. Regarding latency, the excerpt gives one concrete operational comparison rather than a complete measurement of added experimental-cycle time: human operators typically need “minutes” to adjust experimental parameters, whereas the LCLS-II facility can produce data equivalent to an hour of prior collection in only 30 seconds. However, the passage does not specify an exact number of seconds or minutes added per experiment, nor does it provide a measured average intervention duration, frequency of interventions, or total cycle-time increase. Thus, the supported estimate is qualitative to order-of-magnitude level: human adjustment latency is on the scale of minutes, while modern instruments may generate relevant data on the scale of seconds.

contexts.context: The excerpt contrasts a fully automated, closed-loop self-driving laboratory with the more realistic role of a human-in-the-loop. In the default application, the problem, factors, design-space ranges and measurements are fixed in advance, allowing the algorithm to optimize with the human completely out of the loop. However, heterogeneous catalysis commonly involves dozens of potentially relevant factors, making exhaustive exploration impractical. Humans must therefore prioritize which factors to vary and keep others fixed, while scrutinizing those choices as data accumulate. Human intervention may involve recognizing that selected factors are unimportant, identifying previously unexplored relevant factors, changing fixed settings or protocols, introducing or eliminating factors, adapting factor ranges, and imposing safety constraints when experiments reveal hazardous regions. Humans are also needed to interpret trends mechanistically; optimization algorithms identify optima but do not themselves provide the underlying scientific rationale. The excerpt anticipates future algorithms that could make some of these decisions on the fly, including changing factors, adapting ranges and selecting experiments and measurement protocols. It does not report a measured or estimated duration for human decisions, nor does it quantify how much human intervention time or decision latency is added to an experimental cycle. Thus, it supports a qualitative account of human responsibility and intervention, but not a numerical time estimate.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies several consumable-related limits that can restrict unattended self-driving-lab operation. Experimental design spaces may contain points that cannot be explored because chemicals are unavailable or cannot be synthesized. Automated handling of solid reagents is particularly difficult: accurate and precise dispensing becomes challenging for quantities below roughly 20 mg, and discovery-mode workflows involving hundreds of solids may require individualized dispensing settings, making calibration and setup impractical. As a result, many systems avoid direct solid dispensing by using stock solutions and established liquid-handling methods; stock-solution preparation may itself be automated using computer vision. Consumable purification components also create operational risks: disposable solid-phase-extraction cartridges can block or leak and may require human intervention. The excerpt explicitly states that some workflow steps remain dependent on people loading new vials or chemicals into the Chemspeed, which is a direct limitation on fully unattended runs. Proposed future work includes installing robotic arms to imitate human loading actions and adding online process control through computer vision to monitor every operation and detect failures early. The passage does not specify numerical limits on reagent quantities, tip or plate capacity, or a formal restocking schedule; its clearest restocking issue is the need to replenish vials and chemicals manually. It also suggests that equipment and workflows should be redesigned around automation, robust monitoring, and liquid stock solutions.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Context. We run a small cloud lab at BYU (the Vertical Cloud Lab) and are designing a larger autonomous alloy-discovery lab: mobile manipulators (a UR-class arm on a MiR250 base) serving benchtop instruments, a powder atomizer, a desktop laser powder bed fusion printer, characterization and mechanical testing, plus a low-cost AgileX PiPER arm cell for prototyping. Our discrete-event digital twin of that lab concluded that transport does not bind (the robots are 1 to 2 percent busy); what binds is money, the atomizer, a 30-day corrosion immersion, and decision time, with results waiting a median of 77 hours for a person. But every robot handling time in the twin is a stand-in, because nobody has timed a mobile manipulator at our instruments; our alloy team separately estimates 10 to 15 person-hours of hands-on work per atomizer run, also untimed. Our goal is to go from about one alloy tested per day to ten. A citation analysis found that robots restocking consumables is stated as future work in at least six self-driving-lab papers with no follow-up we could find, and that unattended runs are often consumable-limited.

Question.
(1) What measured cycle times and handling times have been published for robot arms and mobile manipulators at laboratory instruments: picking and placing vials, plates and crucibles; docking and re-localizing at a station; loading balances, furnaces, diffractometers, microscopes and tensile testers; opening doors and decapping? Give per-operation means and spread, the robot used (industrial cobot or low-cost arm), and robot idle fractions over campaigns.
(2) Which discrete-event simulations or digital twins of self-driving or automated laboratories used measured rather than assumed handling times, and were any validated against a real campaign? How sensitive was throughput to handling time versus instrument time versus human decision latency?
(3) What has been measured about human decision latency in self-driving labs (waiting for approvals, analysis or the next decision) and what reduced it (asynchronous or batch Bayesian optimization, scheduled decision windows, automated analysis)?
(4) Robots restocking consumables: which systems have robots refill pipette tips, vials, plates, powders, gas or other consumables, with what measured success and unattended run length; and how long have SDL campaigns run before a consumable ran out?
(5) What time-study method should we use to measure our own handling operations for a simulation model (work-measurement methods, number of observations needed for a given precision, how to separate hands-on, waiting and rework time)?

Prefer peer-reviewed sources from 2015 to 2026, and flag preprints. For each claim give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.


## Measured Robot Handling Times, Digital Twins, Human Decision Latency, Consumable Restocking, and Time-Study Methods for Self-Driving Laboratories

This report synthesizes the available peer-reviewed and preprint evidence (2015–2026) across the five questions posed. A key finding is that **published per-operation handling times with statistical spread are extremely scarce**; most SDL papers report aggregate cycle times or campaign-level throughput without isolating individual robot manipulation operations or reporting robot idle fractions. The table below consolidates what has been published.

---

### (1) Measured Cycle Times and Handling Times for Robot Arms and Mobile Manipulators

**Per-step times from materials-science SDLs.** The most granular published step-level timing comes from Xie et al. (2026), who report an automated structural-metallic-materials workflow comprising one robot arm, one induction furnace, one XRD, and one impact tester. Per-sample measured times are: "sample pick-up and loading into the induction furnace takes approximately 60 seconds; weighing the sample and transferring it to the XRD takes 40 seconds; X-ray diffraction measurement and analysis takes 400 seconds; impact testing and analysis takes 120 seconds; and recovery of the fractured sample takes 180 seconds," totaling ≤800 s excluding heat treatment (xie2026developmentofan pages 9-13). No standard deviations or replicate counts are reported for these individual steps.

**Video-derived times from multi-robot PXRD workflows.** Lunt et al. (2023/2024, Chemical Science) describe a 12-step autonomous PXRD workflow using a KUKA KMR iiwa mobile manipulator and an ABB YuMi dual-arm cobot. Video timestamps yield approximate per-operation times: mobile KUKA delivery ≈42 s, diffractometer door opening ≈12 s, plate loading ≈23 s, door closing ≈25 s, and vial-cap manipulation ≈88 s (lunt2023modularmultirobotintegration pages 12-16). These are demonstration-video estimates, not replicated time studies. PXRD acquisition was approximately one hour per sample (lunt2023modularmultirobotintegration pages 12-16).

**Mobile robot transport.** Ali et al. (2018) measured an H20 mobile robot completing a three-station round trip (charge → grasp → place → charge) in a life-science laboratory across 50 runs: mean 15 min 32 s without fine position correction, reduced to mean 11 min 26 s (range 10:46–12:44) with fine correction (ali2018mobilerobottransportation pages 8-9). Separately, the arm motion from rest to the labware manipulation point took approximately 30 seconds (ali2017graspingandplacing pages 8-10). Hernández-del-Valle et al. (2026, preprint) report a TurtleBot4 completing ~96 trips in 6 hours (derived ~3.75 min/trip including charging pauses), and a cobot cell processing 190 polymer specimens in 274 minutes (~86.5 s/specimen including detection, grasping, cutting, and storing) (hernandezdelvalle2026perceptiondrivenexperimentalworkflows pages 10-12).

**Aggregate campaign times.** Ahlquist (2024) measured the MARS SDL experiment at a mean of 86.2 minutes with a coefficient of variation of 2.2% for labware-transportation sub-operations. Parallelization could reduce this to 24.6 minutes (71.4% reduction) (ahlquist2024improvingselfdrivinglabs pages 6-12). Crain et al. (2025) report 84 XRD samples in ~24 h using a Meca500 arm, giving ~17 min/sample including long-exposure measurement; sample changes alone were described as taking "seconds" (crain2025designofa pages 1-5, crain2025designofa pages 5-10). Chu (2016) reports a complete robotic sample-preparation workflow of 81 min 5 s versus 30 min 40 s manually, with pipetting at ~30 mm/s and liquid withdrawal at ~40 mm/s contributing the majority of handling time (chu2016automationstrategiesfor pages 135-138).

**Robot idle fractions.** No retrieved publication reports a measured robot idle fraction or utilization percentage during an SDL campaign. This is a notable gap in the literature.

---

### (2) Discrete-Event Simulations and Digital Twins Using Measured Handling Times

**No validated DES of an SDL using measured handling times was found.** MATTERIX (Darvish et al., 2025, Nature Computational Science) is the closest system: a physics-based digital twin for robotics-assisted chemistry laboratory automation with sim-to-real deployment demonstrations, but the retrieved pages do not report that measured handling-time distributions were used as model inputs, nor is there a quantitative validation against a real experimental campaign comparing predicted and observed throughput (darvish2025matterixtowarda pages 2-5). The MARS system (Ahlquist 2024) timestamped sub-operations and used them to estimate campaign duration and illustrate parallelization opportunities, but this was an empirical timing analysis rather than a formal DES model (ahlquist2024improvingselfdrivinglabs pages 6-12). Zhang et al. (2026) define a reproducibility framework including a "seeded digital twin" for benchmark rollouts and cost functions based on makespan plus penalties, but do not report validation against a real campaign or sensitivity analysis separating handling, instrument, and decision-time effects (zhang2026makingselfdrivinglaboratories pages 8-9).

**Sensitivity analyses.** No retrieved publication performs a formal sensitivity analysis decomposing throughput into contributions from handling time, instrument time, and human decision latency. This represents a significant gap, particularly relevant to the BYU Vertical Cloud Lab's finding that transport does not bind but decision time does.

---

### (3) Human Decision Latency in Self-Driving Labs

**No published study was found that directly measures human decision latency (median or mean waiting time for approvals, analysis, or the next experimental decision) in a self-driving laboratory.** Multiple high-impact papers discuss the role of the human-in-the-loop qualitatively. Scheurer and Reuter (2025, Nature Catalysis) argue that human involvement "should not limit experimental throughput" but provide no measured latency (scheurer2025roleofthe pages 5-5, scheurer2025roleofthe pages 1-2). The ORNL/LCLS workshop report (Silva et al. 2024) provides one quantitative comparison: "human operators typically need 'minutes' to adjust experimental parameters," while modern instruments generate equivalent data in seconds, making human decision-making a potential bottleneck (silva2024shapingthefuture pages 10-12).

**What reduces decision latency.** Several algorithmic approaches have been proposed and benchmarked:

- *Asynchronous Bayesian optimization:* ELF-BO (Sutter et al., 2026, preprint) overlaps MCMC sampling with experimental evaluation, achieving decision latency "close to point-estimate BO and approximately 10 times lower than standard fully Bayesian BO with a Matérn kernel, 70–110 times lower with a deep kernel." On the Photo-WF3 benchmark, standard FBO latency reached up to 24 minutes while ELF-BO remained under 3 seconds (sutter2026workwhilethey pages 1-2, sutter2026workwhilethey pages 9-11).

- *Pipelined batch BO:* Taguchi et al. (2026, SLAS Technology) report that PipeBO "reduced average optimization processing time to approximately 56% of the comparison methods" for two-process experiments on 20 of 24 benchmark functions (taguchi2026asynchronousbatchbayesian pages 1-2).

- *Non-blocking expert feedback:* Kristiadi et al. (2024, preprint) show that asynchronous, intermittent expert feedback on an independent computing thread avoids blocking the BO loop while still improving or constraining optimization (kristiadi2024howusefulis pages 1-3).

- *Asynchronous parallel BO for cloud labs:* Frisby et al. (2021, Bioinformatics) demonstrate PROTOCOL, which "achieves exponential convergence with respect to simple regret" and reduces the number of experiments needed in shared cloud-lab queues (frisby2021asynchronousparallelbayesian pages 1-2).

However, **none of these papers measure how long a human scientist actually takes to review results and approve the next experiment in a physical SDL**. The 77-hour median waiting time mentioned in the user's context appears to be an internal estimate with no published counterpart found in the literature.

---

### (4) Robots Restocking Consumables and Unattended Run Lengths

**No published system was found in which a robot autonomously restocks pipette tips, vials, plates, powders, gas cylinders, or other consumables with measured success rates.** This confirms the user's citation-analysis finding. Multiple papers identify consumable management as a limitation stated as future work:

- Seifrid et al. (2022, Accounts of Chemical Research) explicitly state that "some workflow steps remain dependent on people loading new vials or chemicals into the Chemspeed" and propose "installing robotic arms to imitate human loading actions" as future work (seifrid2022autonomouschemicalexperiments pages 8-9).

- Moran et al. (2026, npj Robotics) propose "autonomous maintenance or 'self-maintainability' (SeM)" as a future concept including labware and device management, but state it "does not yet include autonomous installation and de-installation of robotic hardware" (moran2026theriseof pages 9-11).

- Hernández-del-Valle et al. (2026, preprint) note that injection-molding material "charging and material changes are not automated and therefore require human intervention" (hernandezdelvalle2026perceptiondrivenexperimentalworkflows pages 10-12).

- Müller et al. (2025, preprint/Biotechnology & Bioengineering) report that their bioreactor SDL "still depended on operators for auxiliary consumables and activities, including replenishing liquid containers, at-line analytics, and handling samples for offline analysis" (muller2025selfdrivingdevelopmentof pages 28-31).

**Unattended run lengths.** The longest documented autonomous campaign is the A-Lab (Szymanski et al., 2023, Nature), which operated continuously for 17 days, performing 355 experiments (~20.9 experiments/day) and realizing 41 of 58 target inorganic compounds (szymanski2023anautonomouslaboratory pages 2-3, szymanski2023anautonomouslaboratory pages 4-5). However, the degree to which this was truly unattended (no human restocking or intervention) is not fully described in the retrieved pages. Shorter documented runs include: Hernández-del-Valle et al.'s ~6-hour mobile-robot trial and ~4.5-hour specimen-manipulation demonstration, limited by battery life and material charging (hernandezdelvalle2026perceptiondrivenexperimentalworkflows pages 10-12); and Ahlquist's MARS campaigns, where prior campaign failure rates were 29–43% before gripper improvements reduced them to 4.4–7.2% (ahlquist2024improvingselfdrivinglabs pages 6-12, ahlquist2024improvingselfdrivinglabs pages 1-6).

**Consumable-limited factors.** Tegally et al. (2020, BMC Genomics) explicitly quantify tip consumption for a 96-library genomics preparation: "1,920 50-µL Hamilton tips, 576 300-µL tips, and 25 1,000-µL tips," demonstrating that deck consumable capacity directly limits unattended run length (tegally2020unlockingtheefficiency pages 11-12). Evaporation during long protocols is also identified as a consumable-management challenge (tegally2020unlockingtheefficiency pages 11-12).
